attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post. They describe the OpenAI submission reported by the Telegraph.

semantics.note: The proposition captures his characterisation of the lobbying campaign as a false dichotomy plus a threat. It is heavily interpretive, but the factual core can be checked against the submission's text.

contract.note: Testing whether the submission tied AI's survival to free access and left licensing out is a fair reading of his charge. The result depends on reading the full submission, which the packet lacks.

evidence.note: Partial Guardian report. It says OpenAI called training without copyrighted material impossible, but it does not show whether OpenAI demanded free access or left licensing out.
A separate OpenAI blog post (company disclosure) claiming fair use and citing partnerships. It is not the UK submission, so it does not settle what the submission argued.

reviews.rationale: The original submission could not be read. The reporting that was read confirms OpenAI said copyrighted material was necessary, but not whether it framed the choice as free access or no generative AI, or excluded licensing. The evidence does not settle either the support or the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The checkable core is that OpenAI was pursuing licensing deals. The charge that the argument is disingenuous is evaluative and cannot be verified.

contract.note: Grading only the factual licensing core, and setting aside the accusation of intent, is a fair and ordinary reading.

evidence.note: AP, the counterparty, confirms in July 2023 that OpenAI licensed part of its text archive, before the post.
OpenAI's own announcement from December 2023 of the Axel Springer partnership, which includes use of content for training. This was before the post.

reviews.rationale: Two dated records before the post show OpenAI making content-licensing deals: AP in July 2023 and Axel Springer in December 2023. That meets the support condition. The claim that OpenAI knew its argument was false is not graded and is not established.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: In context, he means current AI that performs reasonably well depends on internet-scale data. The 'not a logical necessity' qualifier is preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading, needing internet-scale data to learn useful capabilities, is fair. Counting narrow grammar learning by a tiny model as 'useful capability' would stretch it against the speaker.

evidence.note: Baby Llama learns some linguistic competence from 10M words. It does not show useful generative capability without large data, and the paper itself calls current LMs far less sample-efficient than humans.
Llama 2 was trained on 2T tokens. This shows the scale used, not that such scale is necessary.

reviews.rationale: No item shows internet-scale data was necessary, so the support condition is not met. Baby Llama's small-corpus results cover narrow grammar benchmarks, not the reasonably performing systems Marcus describes, so they do not clearly meet the contradiction condition. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The factual core is that open LLMs had already been released and many people had the expertise to build them. 'The threat is empty' is an inference he draws from that.

contract.note: Reading the claim as publicly usable model releases plus a substantial builder community, with no numeric threshold, is ordinary and fair. The contract scores only that factual core.

evidence.note: Mistral 7B was released under Apache 2.0 in September 2023 with instructions for local use. This is a company disclosure, but adequate for the fact that the release happened.
The BLOOM report, available June 2023, documents over 1,200 participants, hundreds of whom contributed directly to building an open LLM.

reviews.rationale: Records from before the post show a publicly usable open LLM (Mistral 7B, Apache 2.0) and a large collaborative builder community (BigScience/BLOOM). That meets the support condition. The broader 'empty threat' inference is evaluative and is not separately graded.
